title: Runtime cost / SLO balancing and eviction policy playbook
author: Priya Raman
body:
SUMMARY
This playbook defines an operator-facing, testable procedure for balancing runtime cost controls against latency and availability SLOs in private VPC/on‑prem deployments. It prescribes an eviction policy taxonomy, decision thresholds, telemetry contracts, and runbook steps for safe enforcement and rollback. It focuses on tenant-facing inference services (runtime-proxy, gpu-scheduler, kv-cache) and is intended for field operators, SREs, and operator automation engineers.

Why this exists
- Private deployments often run heterogeneous workloads with conflicting economics: some tenants require low p95 latency, others tolerate higher latency but need high throughput.
- When capacity or thermal constraints occur, automated eviction/throttling mitigations protect critical SLOs but must avoid unnecessary cost overruns and customer impact.
- This playbook provides a deterministic policy set operators can deploy and a validation checklist for upgrades.

Scope
- Applies to: VPC / on‑prem Redwood Private environments, dedicated GPU clusters managed by runtime-controller and tenant-quota-service.
- Not covered: model artifact build pipelines, long-term billing reconciliation (finance maintains separate docs).

Goals
1) Protect critical latency SLOs (p95 <= configured target) for priority tenants while containing GPU spend growth.
2) Provide predictable, auditable eviction decisions with forensic telemetry.
3) Ensure safe rollback and customer notification paths.

Key concepts and terminology
- Priority class: tenant priority label (critical | standard | best-effort). Set by customer contract via onboarding.
- Eviction window: short timeframe (usually 60–300s) where tenant tokens / requests are preferentially throttled or rejected.
- Graceful degradation: service-level fallback (quantized model, lower beam, reduced response length).
- Burst absorber: a local admission controller that uses token-bucket + predictive de‑queueing to smooth spikes.

SLO / cost mapping matrix (example)
| Priority | Target p95 latency | Allowed throughput loss | Preemptible GPU use | Billing tier |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| critical | <= 120ms | 0% | no | SLA: gold |
| standard | <= 250ms | up to 10% | yes (if warm) | SLA: silver |
| best-effort | <= 500ms | up to 30% | yes (immediate) | SLA: bronze |

Eviction policy taxonomy
1. Soft throttling (request-level): reduce admission via burst absorber. Preferred initial step.
2. Graceful fallback (model-level): switch to a quantized or truncated variant with known cost profile.
3. Tenant-level preemption: move non-critical tenant workloads to preemptible nodes / spot capacity.
4. Eviction (hard): terminate or deny new requests until load reduces. Use with explicit operator approval for critical tenants.

Decision thresholds (recommended starting point)
- Node GPU utilization sustained > 88% for 3 minutes -> trigger soft throttling for best-effort tenants.
- p95 latency for priority class critical exceeds target by >20% for 90s -> escalate to graceful fallback for non-critical replicas; notify oncall.
- Control-plane queue depth > 10k and mean request wait > 250ms -> enable tenant-level preemption policies.
- Thermal throttling (hardware telemetry) detected on > 1/3 of nodes in a zone -> immediate admission control and operator alert.

Telemetry and observability contract (what must be emitted)
- Per-tenant: p50/p95/p99, request rate, rejection rate, average token cost, model variant in use, priority_class label. Emit at 10s resolution.
- Per-node: GPU util, memory pressure, temperature, power draw, active model slots, last eviction timestamp. Emit at 5s resolution for critical nodes.
- Control-plane: admission decisions (reason code), last policy evaluation, operator override flag.
- Audit logs: immutable entries for any hard eviction or tenant preemption including timestamp, initiator (auto/operator), justification, and trace id.

Operator runbook: handling an ongoing capacity/latency incident
1) Triage (0–3 minutes)
   a) Confirm alert: check runtime-dashboard, per-tenant p95, node GPU util.
   b) Identify impacted priority classes (query: tenant-quota-service /api/v1/tenants?priority=true).
2) Apply safe mitigations (3–10 minutes)
   a) Enable soft throttling via: curl -X POST "https://control-plane.local/api/adm/burst-absorber" -d '{"action":"enable","scope":"best-effort"}'
   b) Flip graceful fallback flag for target tenants:
      - CLI: rctl tenant set-variant --tenant-id TID --variant quantized-small --timeout 10m
   c) Monitor p95 over 30s windows. If p95 improves, continue observation.
3) Escalate to preemption (10–30 minutes)
   a) If sustained GPU util > 90% and latencies remain degraded, enact tenant preemptions using the preemption API with a dry-run first:
      - rctl preempt --target-class best-effort --dry-run=true
   b) Notify stakeholders (email + slack #ops) with template: "Preemption dry-run performed at TIMESTAMP for class best-effort. See trace TR-XXXX."
4) Hard eviction and customer communication (30+ minutes)
   a) Only with operator approval and when other mitigations failed. Record justification and runbook checklist in incident ticket.
   b) Execute: rctl eviction start --tenant-id TID --reason "capacity-critical" --expected-duration 15m
   c) Generate audit package and notify customer success to issue escalation communication.

Post-incident forensics and cost reconciliation
- Produce an incident report with: timeline, policy decisions, telemetry extracts (per-tenant, per-node), and cost delta for the interval.
- For each hard eviction, attach: operator approval snapshot, preemption dry-run results, and the rollback sequence used.

Safety nets and rollback patterns
- Operator override: any automated eviction can be paused with the operator-override flag (control-plane API). Overrides must be time-limited (max 1h) and logged.
- Canary: test eviction policy in a canary namespace for 24h with synthetic load before wide rollout. Use tenant-sim harness (see testing).
- Automatic revert: if p95 for priority-critical increases by > 15% post-policy change, automatic rollback to last policy config after 60s.

Testing and validation checklist (pre-deploy)
1) Unit tests for policy evaluation logic (simulate load patterns).
2) Integration tests: end-to-end with runtime-proxy, gpu-scheduler, and tenant-quota-service using staged models.
3) Chaos tests: simulate node loss, thermal events, and control-plane network partition. Verify correct admission and audit logs.
4) Cost simulation: run a 6h synthetic workload to model GPU-hour impact of policy choices.

Example policy config (YAML)
policy_name: balanced-2026
description: "Default policy for mixed-priority clusters"
priority_classes:
  - name: critical
    p95_target_ms: 120
    preempt_allowed: false
  - name: standard
    p95_target_ms: 250
    preempt_allowed: true
  - name: best-effort
    p95_target_ms: 500
    preempt_allowed: true
admission_controls:
  burst_absorber:
    enabled: true
    token_rate: 1000
    burst_size: 2000
eviction_rules:
  - trigger: node_gpu_utilization
    threshold: 88
    sustained_seconds: 180

Operator CLI quick reference
- Check per-tenant latency: rctl metrics tenant p95 --tenant TID --window 1m
- Toggle soft throttling: rctl admission set --burst-absorber {enable|disable} --scope {best-effort|standard|all}
- Start preempt dry-run: rctl preempt --target-class best-effort --dry-run

Rollout and change process
1) Draft policy PR in config-repo. Include test plan and cost simulation output.
2) Create canary namespace in staging; run 24h synthetic load (synth-tool run --policy balanced-2026 --namespace canary).
3) After successful canary, schedule progressive rollout to one cluster at a time during low-business-hours.
4) Post-rollout: collect telemetry for 72h and sign off if stable.

Ownership and escalation
- Policy owner: runtime-ops (oncall: runtime-ops@redwood.example.com)
- SRE escalation: eng-sre oncall if incident impacts multiple clusters or region.
- Customer communication: customer-success pager and account lead for any tenant-facing hard eviction.

Templates
- Customer notification (short): "We applied temporary capacity measures that may have affected non-critical requests; your SLA for critical requests remains intact. Contact cust-success@redwood.example.com with ticket ID."
- Incident recording checklist: incident_id, start_time, policy_version, affected_tenants, mitigation_steps, approval_signatures.

Appendix: example telemetry query (Influx/PromQL style)
- p95 per tenant: max_over_time(histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_bucket[1m])) by (le, tenant))[5m:1m])
- node GPU util: avg(node_gpu_utilization{zone=~"us-*"}) by (node)

References and related docs
- Onboarding contract fields that define priority_class (see customer-requirements-library).
- Runtime admission control API spec (internal link).

FAQ
Q: Can we evict critical tenants?
A: Only with explicit operator approval and documented justification. In most cases we prefer graceful fallback or preemption to spot instances.

Q: How do cost savings measure against customer impact?
A: All policy changes require a cost delta simulation; production change must include SLA impact analysis.
